clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of adenosine deaminase, a purine-degradation enzyme, causing toxic accumulation of adenosine and deoxyadenosine and the most common metabolic cause of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
Classic early-onset disease presents in the first months of life with profound lymphopenia affecting T, B and NK cells, recurrent severe infections, chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive.

Unlike other forms of SCID, ADA deficiency is a systemic metabolic disorder with non-immune features including skeletal abnormalities (costochondral cupping), sensorineural deafness and neurodevelopmental problems.
Delayed and partial-activity phenotypes exist, presenting in later childhood or adulthood with milder recurrent infections and autoimmunity, so a normal early history does not exclude the diagnosis.
Accumulated deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated to deoxyadenosine triphosphate, which is especially toxic to lymphocytes; erythrocyte dATP is markedly raised and ADA activity is very low or absent.
Newborn screening for SCID by T-cell receptor excision circle assay detects most affected infants before infections occur, enabling early treatment.

Treatment options include enzyme replacement with pegylated ADA, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and autologous gene therapy; strict infection prophylaxis and avoidance of live vaccines are essential.
Irradiated, cytomegalovirus-safe blood products must be used and live vaccines withheld until immune reconstitution is confirmed.
reference.pathophysiology: Adenosine deaminase is a ubiquitous enzyme of purine catabolism that deaminates adenosine to inosine and deoxyadenosine to deoxyinosine. Loss of function leads to intracellular and extracellular accumulation of these substrates. Deoxyadenosine is taken up and phosphorylated by deoxycytidine kinase to deoxyadenosine triphosphate, which accumulates to very high concentrations in lymphoid tissue; dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and impairs DNA synthesis and repair, while also promoting apoptosis of developing and mature lymphocytes. The result is a combined deficiency of T, B and NK cells with both quantitative lymphopenia and functional impairment. Because the enzyme defect is systemic rather than confined to the immune system, elevated purine metabolites also injure non-immune tissues, producing the characteristic skeletal, neurological, hepatic and pulmonary manifestations that distinguish ADA deficiency from other genetic causes of SCID. Residual enzyme activity correlates broadly with the age of onset and severity, so hypomorphic variants give rise to delayed or partial phenotypes with later, milder immunodeficiency and a tendency to autoimmunity and elevated immunoglobulin E.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic forms of severe combined immunodeficiency (e.g. X-linked common gamma chain, JAK3, IL7R, RAG defects)
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency (predominantly T-cell defect with neurological features)
DiGeorge syndrome and other thymic developmental defects
Congenital or acquired causes of failure to thrive with recurrent infection
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase enzyme activity assay
Measurement of erythrocyte deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP) and related metabolites
Lymphocyte subset enumeration by flow cytometry (T, B and NK cells)
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses
Molecular genetic testing of the ADA gene
Newborn screening T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) result where available
Skeletal survey for costochondral and other bony changes; hearing assessment
redFlags: Profound lymphopenia or absent thymic shadow in an infant with recurrent infection
Opportunistic infection such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or disseminated viral or fungal disease
Failure to thrive with chronic diarrhoea in early infancy
Administration of a live vaccine or non-irradiated blood product to an undiagnosed infant
Signs of maternal engraftment or graft-versus-host reaction
reference.prognosis: Untreated early-onset ADA-SCID is usually fatal within the first years of life from infection. Early definitive treatment with stem cell transplantation, enzyme replacement or gene therapy can restore immune function and give good survival, though systemic non-immune complications may persist.
pitfalls: Assuming all SCID is purely immunological and overlooking the systemic metabolic features unique to ADA deficiency
Excluding the diagnosis because presentation is delayed or relatively mild in partial-activity variants
Giving live vaccines or non-irradiated, cytomegalovirus-unsafe blood products before the diagnosis is excluded
Interpreting erythrocyte ADA activity without accounting for recent transfusion, which can mask deficiency
Delaying referral for definitive therapy while awaiting resolution of infections
references: Standard textbook of inborn errors of metabolism
Clinical immunology reference texts on primary immunodeficiency
International guidance on severe combined immunodeficiency
management: Offer haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally from a matched donor, as the definitive curative treatment
Consider autologous gene therapy with gene-corrected haematopoietic stem cells where available
Use enzyme replacement with polyethylene-glycol-conjugated adenosine deaminase (pegademase or elapegademase) as a bridge or when transplantation and gene therapy are not options
Give infection prophylaxis against Pneumocystis, fungi and viruses, and replace immunoglobulin with regular infusions
Institute protective isolation, use irradiated cytomegalovirus-negative blood products and avoid live vaccines
Support nutrition and growth to address failure to thrive and treat chronic diarrhoea
Monitor immune reconstitution and metabolite levels after definitive treatment
Provide genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive disorder, using newborn screening to identify affected infants before infections occur
